meta.title: Who really said "Fathers Should Give the Gift of Time to Their Children"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Ann Landers — and not a quotation. It is an anonymous 1956 poem, “Give Him a Day”, that Landers reprinted in her column in 1988.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Fathers Should Give the Gift of Time to Their Children'?
meta.ogDescription: Nobody said it. It is the title of a research article about an anonymous 1956 Father’s Day poem, which Ann Landers reprinted without an author in 1988.

answer.label: Not Ann Landers — an anonymous poem she reprinted
answer.authorName: Unknown — an anonymous Father’s Day poem
answer.authorDates: In print by June 1956 · author never identified
answer.sourceLine: Two things to untangle here. First, this sentence is not a quotation — it is the headline of Quote Investigator’s article about the verse ↗, written by the researcher, not by anybody being quoted. Second, the verse itself is anonymous: it was running in American newspapers around Father’s Day by 6 June 1956, under the title “Give Him a Day”, and QI found it labelled anonymous in every 1956–57 printing it located. Ann Landers reprinted it in her syndicated column on 11 June 1988 — sent in by a reader, with no author name given — which is how her byline came to be attached to it.

source.excerpt: What shall you give to one small boy? A glamorous game, a tinseled toy, A barlow knife, a puzzle pack, A train that runs on curving track? A picture book; a real live pet. No, there’s plenty of time for such things yet. Give him a day for his very own— Just one small boy and his dad alone. A walk in the woods, a romp in the park, A fishing trip from dawn to dark. Give the gift that only you can— The companionship of his Old Man. Games are outgrown, and toys decay— But he’ll never forget if you “Give him a day.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ locates the earliest printing in the Oxnard Press-Courier of 6 June 1956, page 1, and records that “the author was anonymous”. Its conclusion is explicit: “The author was unidentified in all the cites located by QI.”

The same article lists three further newspaper printings in the following months — the Logansport Press (Indiana) in 1956, the Millbrook Round Table (New York) in April 1957 and the Augusta Chronicle (Georgia) in June 1957 — noting that “each time the poem was labeled anonymous”.

For the Ann Landers connection, QI cites her column of 11 June 1988 in The Spokesman-Review / Spokane Chronicle, page C2, under the title “In lieu of toys, give son some time”, where she introduces the verse as a reader’s submission and gives no author name.

The column that carried it in 1988 was written by Esther “Eppie” Lederer ↗, who had used the Ann Landers pen name since 1955; the column itself ↗ was created by Ruth Crowley in 1943. Neither wrote the poem.
source.excerptNote: The 1956 Oxnard Press-Courier text, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. The 1988 version Ann Landers printed differs in small ways — “barlow knife” had become “Boy Scout knife” — which is the ordinary drift of a poem passed hand to hand for three decades.

source.rightsNote: quotle.info asserts no rights status for this verse. It was first published in 1956 — well after the 1931 United States public-domain cutoff — so it cannot simply be assumed to be free; but its author has never been identified, so there is no author, estate or publisher to name as a rights holder either. Anonymity is not the same thing as public domain, and a newspaper poem of 1956 may or may not have passed into it depending on notice and renewal, which we have not established. The verse is quoted here in full for comment and criticism on exactly the question of its authorship.

author.name: Ann Landers
author.heading: About Ann Landers
author.metaLine: Pen name, created 1943 · American newspaper advice column
author.bio: Ann Landers was never one person. The pen name was created by the Chicago Sun-Times columnist Ruth Crowley in 1943 and taken over in 1955 by Esther “Eppie” Lederer (1918–2002), who wrote it for forty-seven years to a readership of some ninety million. A column that ran every day lived on what readers mailed in — poems, jokes, homilies, mostly unsigned — and reprinting them under a famous byline is how a great many anonymous pieces, this poem among them, ended up credited to her.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This one is misattributed twice over: a research headline gets read as a quotation, and a column that reprinted a poem gets read as having written it.

items.why: Her 1988 column is where most readers met the verse, and she wrote “I hope every father who reads it will want to keep this copy” — the words of someone passing something on. QI records that the poem reached her from a reader and carried no author name ↗, and that it had already been in newspapers for thirty-two years.

items.who: “Fathers should give the gift of time to their children”
items.tag: Not a quotation — a research headline
items.why: These words appear in no newspaper, no column and no poem. They are the title Quote Investigator gave its own article, in the site’s house style of capitalising headlines. Quoting them as though someone said them, and then attaching a speaker, manufactures a quotation out of a bibliography entry.
Four separate newspapers printed the poem in 1956 and 1957 and not one named a writer. QI located no attribution in any citation. The honest answer to “who wrote this?” is that nobody knows.

The 1956 text has a “barlow knife”; by 1988 it was a “Boy Scout knife”, and a 1994 anthology had replaced the closing couplet with “Give the best gift to that bright lad— The companionship of his dear dad.” An anonymous poem with no copyright owner to object drifts freely.

misattribution.truthLine: The verse is an anonymous American Father’s Day poem, “Give Him a Day”, in print by 6 June 1956. Ann Landers reprinted it in 1988 and named no author, because she had none to name — as Quote Investigator documents ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The poem is a small piece of mid-century newspaper filler that worked: a list of presents a father might buy, each rejected, ending on the one thing he cannot buy. Papers ran it in the week before Father’s Day because it fitted a column inch and said the thing everybody wanted said, and readers clipped it out, which is why it kept reappearing.

Clipping is also how it lost its author. A poem that travels by scissors and envelope arrives with no byline attached, and the last person to print it inherits the credit. Ann Landers was simply the most famous link in a chain that had been running for three decades.
detailsBody: The reader who wrote to Quote Investigator remembered the poem from an Ann Landers column and misremembered one line, recalling a “tinker toy” where the 1956 text has a “tinseled toy”. That is a fair illustration of how the verse survived: in people’s memories and in cuttings, not in any book of record.

Worth separating the two claims this page handles, because they fail differently. “Ann Landers wrote this” is false and can be shown false. “Fathers should give the gift of time to their children” is not false, it is simply not a quotation — it is a description of a poem, written in 2012 by a researcher, which has since been passed around inside quotation marks.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest printing QI located is the Oxnard Press-Courier (Oxnard, California), 6 June 1956, page 1, where the poem's author was anonymous; the text given includes 'Give him a day for his very own—Just one small boy and his dad alone.'

QI lists further printings in the Logansport Press (Indiana, 1956), Millbrook Round Table (New York, 1957) and Augusta Chronicle (Georgia, 1957), stating that each time the poem was labeled anonymous, and concludes the author was unidentified in all cites located.

Ann Landers reprinted the verse on 11 June 1988 in The Spokesman-Review / Spokane Chronicle, page C2, under 'In lieu of toys, give son some time', from a reader's submission, giving no author name, with 'barlow knife' altered to 'Boy Scout knife'.
Esther Pauline "Eppie" Lederer (4 July 1918 - 22 June 2002) wrote the Ask Ann Landers column under that pen name from 1955 for 47 years.
Ruth Crowley created the Chicago Sun-Times "Ask Ann Landers" column, writing it intermittently from 1943 until her death in 1955.
